{"id": "28:27/q19", "question": "How are reported sheep traits explained?", "turns_on": "Report glosses differ for two animal terms.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q19/p1", "position": "The lamb reward excluded sheep with several deficient milking traits.", "reasons": "Harawi lists the exclusion; Ibn Kathir prefers wording that says deficient types were absent."}, {"id": "28:27/q19/p2", "position": "ʿAzūz has little or narrow milk flow.", "reasons": "Harawi relates it to hard ground; Ibn Lahiʿa says narrow flow."}, {"id": "28:27/q19/p3", "position": "Fashūsh leaks milk freely through a broad passage.", "reasons": "Harawi adds idioms and a hadith image; Ibn Lahiʿa agrees on a large flow."}, {"id": "28:27/q19/p4", "position": "Kumush or kumaysha has a small contracted udder.", "reasons": "Harawi mentions kushud and kamish al-izar; Ibn Lahiʿa says too small to grasp."}, {"id": "28:27/q19/p5", "position": "Dabūb has a narrow milk opening or a long dragging udder.", "reasons": "Harawi says dab means forceful milking; Ibn Lahiʿa gives the divergent long-udder sense."}, {"id": "28:27/q19/p6", "position": "Thaʿūl has an extra teat, or an extremely reduced udder.", "reasons": "Harawi also explains extra tooth and narrow passage; Ibn Lahiʿa describes something like two teats."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q20", "question": "Is payment in future lambs a valid hire?", "turns_on": "Whether uncertain yield is acceptable compensation.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q20/p1", "position": "No: births and survival are uncertain wages.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites prohibition of uncertain sale and unborn offspring in wombs or loins."}, {"id": "28:27/q20/p2", "position": "A share of flock offspring or of woven cloth can compensate labor.", "reasons": "Rashid permits one-third or one-quarter of offspring; Ibn Sirin, Ata and Ahmad allow a weaver's share."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q21", "question": "What does the optional ten-year completion mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the offer is framed as fixed eight plus gift or a stated choice.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q21/p1", "position": "The extra two years are Moses's voluntary favor beyond the required eight.", "reasons": "The commentaries repeatedly stress this; Ibn Ashur says Moses could decide after eight; Biqai connects the years to maturation and observing a grandson."}, {"id": "28:27/q21/p2", "position": "The offer states a choice of eight or ten years.", "reasons": "Tabatabai uses this formulation but denies the father could require ten."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q22", "question": "How is 'from you' analyzed?", "turns_on": "The ellipsis may be nominal or verbal.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q22/p1", "position": "It means from Moses's favor, outside the employer's claim.", "reasons": "Damghani and Burhan gloss generosity; Ibn Ashur calls min partitive, ʿinda figurative self, with omitted predicate."}, {"id": "28:27/q22/p2", "position": "It may predicate omitted 'it is' or imply the verb 'you added it'.", "reasons": "Samin gives nominal and accusative analyses."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q23", "question": "Which term did Moses actually complete?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on whether he stayed another decade.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q23/p1", "position": "The longer, better ten-year term.", "reasons": "Gabriel, Prophetic reports, Ibn Abbas and Ja'far al-Sadiq say this; Ibn Kathir says mursal routes reinforce each other, though al-Bazzar finds the Abu Dharr chain singular. Ibn Abbas says a prophet fulfills the better term."}, {"id": "28:27/q23/p2", "position": "Ten years of service followed by ten more years' stay.", "reasons": "Mujahid reports this additional period."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q24", "question": "Why did Moses hire himself out?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q24/p1", "position": "To preserve chastity and obtain food.", "reasons": "Reports in Ibn Abi Hatim, Mawardi, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Durr say this; Ibn Kathir calls one Utba route weak due to Maslama ibn Ali and questions another; he doubts Ibn Lahiʿa's raised report."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q25", "question": "What hardship does the father disclaim?", "turns_on": "The assurance may concern the extra years, the work, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q25/p1", "position": "He will not demand the full ten years.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Wahidi, Baghawi and others say so."}, {"id": "28:27/q25/p2", "position": "He will be lenient about daily work, scrutiny and extra duties.", "reasons": "Kashshaf compares strict employers; Razi mentions excessive care; Tabatabai says he presents as a good employer; Ibn Ashur cites gracious trade."}, {"id": "28:27/q25/p3", "position": "No part of the agreement, required or optional, is meant to be onerous.", "reasons": "Biqai gives this wider reading."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q26", "question": "What is the image behind 'ashuq'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q26/p1", "position": "A hard task seems to split one's judgment over ability to bear it.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Samin, Bursevi and Alusi give the root image; Ibn Ashur says the employer would cause the burden."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q27", "question": "What is promised by being among the righteous?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective is contextual or general.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q27/p1", "position": "Good companionship, gentleness, fair treatment and keeping the covenant.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites Moses's counsel to Aaron at 7:142; Ibn Ishaq, Umar and later commentators stress fidelity and kind dealing; Ibn Ashur calls it character disclosure."}, {"id": "28:27/q27/p2", "position": "General righteousness, including good dealings.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi and Nasafi allow this broader sense; Asad notes the literal 'one of the righteous'."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q28", "question": "Why is the promise qualified by 'if God wills'?", "turns_on": "The sources differ over what is conditioned.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q28/p1", "position": "For blessing and reliance on divine help, without doubting his intention.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi, Bursevi and Alusi say this; Alusi compares al-Shafii's 'I am a believer, God willing'."}, {"id": "28:27/q28/p2", "position": "The speaker might die before fulfilling his promise.", "reasons": "Tabrisi makes uncertain survival the point."}, {"id": "28:27/q28/p3", "position": "The qualification concerns Moses finding him righteous, not whether he is righteous.", "reasons": "Tabatabai assigns this grammatical scope."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q29", "question": "How are the opening hamzas read?", "turns_on": "The hamza at the word boundary differs.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q29/p1", "position": "The standard reading retains the iḥdā hamza, with ordinary waṣl elision and nūn ḍamma.", "reasons": "The Qiraat-ER segments give standard Hafs forms."}, {"id": "28:27/q29/p2", "position": "Warsh and Ahmad ibn Musa from Abu Amr omit the hamza across unkiḥaka iḥdā.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi report it; Samin compares Ibn Muhaysin at 28:25."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q30", "question": "How is the nūn of hātayn read?", "turns_on": "The nūn is light or doubled.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q30/p1", "position": "A single nūn is standard.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER gives the standard form."}, {"id": "28:27/q30/p2", "position": "A variant geminates the nūn.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER and al-Nashr report it; Ibn Kathir geminates five analogous forms, with Abu Amr and Ruways agreeing in one."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q31", "question": "How are the possessive yāʾs read?", "turns_on": "Transmission and morphology govern the vocalization.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q31/p1", "position": "The two Medinan readers open both yāʾs.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid says Nafi opens nearly all twelve listed cases; al-Nashr specifies both phrases."}, {"id": "28:27/q31/p2", "position": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr leave these two yāʾs quiescent.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid lists them among three exceptions to nine opened cases."}, {"id": "28:27/q31/p3", "position": "Opening is obligatory in certain noun forms, otherwise reading transmission permits opening or quiescence.", "reasons": "Samarrai states the general rule."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q32", "question": "Does the father act as marriage guardian, and may he offer a daughter?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrative establishes a mandatory guardian.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q32/p1", "position": "A guardian contracts marriage and may offer his daughter to a worthy man.", "reasons": "Qurtubi compares Umar offering Hafsa to Uthman and a woman offering herself to the Prophet; major jurists and Abu Hayyan read a guardian role."}, {"id": "28:27/q32/p2", "position": "An adult competent woman may contract her own marriage in some cases.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa disputes an absolute guardian requirement."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q33", "question": "May a father marry an adult virgin without asking her?", "turns_on": "Whether narrative silence proves absence of consent.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q33/p1", "position": "Yes, without prior consultation.", "reasons": "Malik and Shafii use the offer; Qurtubi calls Malik's argument strong but notes reliance on Israelite reports."}, {"id": "28:27/q33/p2", "position": "An adult woman's consent is required; silence here does not show it was absent.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa distinguishes minors; Ibn Ashur records opponents' reply that permission may have occurred unmentioned."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q34", "question": "Which formula can validly contract marriage?", "turns_on": "Whether specific Quranic marriage verbs are necessary.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q34/p1", "position": "Only nikah or tazwij wording.", "reasons": "Shafii's followers, Rabiʿa and others argue so; Abu Umar requires explicit speech before witnesses, rejecting divorce analogy. Qurtubi says the verse as earlier law does not prove it."}, {"id": "28:27/q34/p2", "position": "Clear permanent-transfer or gift wording can suffice.", "reasons": "The well-known Maliki position is broad; Abu Hani

{"id": "28:27/q35", "question": "What other contract rulings are drawn from the episode?", "turns_on": "These are distinct analogies and adjacent legal deductions.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q35/p1", "position": "An addition to agreed consideration can be valid.", "reasons": "Jurists cite the two optional years; Razi cautions that an earlier law does not bind."}, {"id": "28:27/q35/p2", "position": "A sale of one of two slaves for one price can be valid.", "reasons": "Hanafi jurists use the unnamed daughter analogy."}, {"id": "28:27/q35/p3", "position": "Alternative cash and deferred prices can be valid.", "reasons": "Al-Awzai invokes the verse and two-sales hadith; Ibn Kathir questions the inference."}, {"id": "28:27/q35/p4", "position": "Hiring for food and clothing is valid.", "reasons": "Ahmad's followers infer it from Moses's employment."}, {"id": "28:27/q35/p5", "position": "Permissible poetry teaching may be dowry; obscene poetry may not.", "reasons": "Al-Muzani cites a pious poem; Qurtubi compares obscene content to wine or pork."}, {"id": "28:27/q35/p6", "position": "Marriage compatibility is legally relevant, though its criteria differ.", "reasons": "Qurtubi lists religion, wealth and lineage disputes and permits non-Arab clients to marry Arab or Qurayshi women."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q36", "question": "How is Moses's staff said to have come to him and acted?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on staff origin and miracles.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q36/p1", "position": "Gabriel preserved Adam's paradisal staff and handed it to Moses.", "reasons": "Ikrima reports the heavenly origin."}, {"id": "28:27/q36/p2", "position": "Prophets inherited the staff until Shuayb gave it to Moses.", "reasons": "Other authorities and al-Qushayri connect it to Adam."}, {"id": "28:27/q36/p3", "position": "An angel entrusted it to Shuayb; Moses repeatedly selected and alone lifted it.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi describes the daughter fetching only this staff and an angel arbitrating ownership."}, {"id": "28:27/q36/p4", "position": "Yathrun's thirteen staffs killed eleven sons sent to retrieve one, but Moses took his.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says Yathrun recognized Moses as a prophet."}, {"id": "28:27/q36/p5", "position": "The staff killed a dragon and returned bloody.", "reasons": "Thalabi says Moses saw a divine sign and Shuayb found the sheep healthier; al-Qushayri relates the dragon too."}, {"id": "28:27/q36/p6", "position": "God gave Shuayb Moses as servant after Shuayb wept blind from love of God.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits the account."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q37", "question": "How does this episode connect to the larger narrative?", "turns_on": "Sources relate the verse to prayer, repetition, ethics and sura setting.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q37/p1", "position": "It answers Moses's prayers for safety, guidance and provision.", "reasons": "Tabatabai links the Midian road, work, wife and ten years' livelihood to 28:21."}, {"id": "28:27/q37/p2", "position": "Repeated Moses stories vary in wording and order to convey distinct nuances.", "reasons": "Burhan contrasts the dispersed Moses account with Joseph's collected story."}, {"id": "28:27/q37/p3", "position": "It displays virtues preparing Moses for revelation and models character.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur names generosity, aid, modesty, gratitude, chastity and fidelity; Shuayb shows hospitality and gentleness; Meccans could compare Muhammad."}, {"id": "28:27/q37/p4", "position": "The offer illustrates a natural wish for increase.", "reasons": "Qurtubi compares Sa'd, Joseph's brothers at 12:65 and Job."}, {"id": "28:27/q37/p5", "position": "It follows the daughter's suggestion in 28:25.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu connects the agreement to her advice."}, {"id": "28:27/q37/p6", "position": "Al-Qasas is wholly Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi transmits al-Hasan, Ata and Ikrima on the sura's revelation."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q38", "question": "What inward reading is given to marriage and years of service?", "turns_on": "People and years are mapped onto spiritual faculties and stages.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q38/p1", "position": "Marriage brings the daughter under the heart's command for holy light and unveiling.", "reasons": "Qashani gives this inward mapping."}, {"id": "28:27/q38/p2", "position": "Eight years symbolize eight stages of annihilation and witnessing; ten add annihilation in Essence and subsistence.", "reasons": "Qashani cites 7:143 and Abraham's ten perfections at 2:124; Bursevi reports completion at eight and fuller perfection at ten, linking Moses's age thirty and later call."}, {"id": "28:27/q38/p3", "position": "Serving Shuayb images the seeker leaving the commanding soul for the heart and serving a guide.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites Ibrahim ibn Adham's seventeen years of wood-carrying and a Hafiz couplet on devoted service."}, {"id": "28:27/q38/p4", "position": "Fidelity in service follows one beyond death.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites the Mathnawi."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q39", "question": "What incidental grammatical and scholarly examples appear with these notes?", "turns_on": "These retrieved passages are contextual rather than explanations of the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q39/p1", "position": "Thamānī is among examples of final-yāʾ treatment before a nisba suffix.", "reasons": "Sibawayh compares nājī, adlī and ṣaḥārī; Khalil and Yunus discuss optional fatḥ and poetic ḥānawī."}, {"id": "28:27/q39/p2", "position": "Exclamations can take accusative specification and emphatic min.", "reasons": "Sibawayh discusses wayḥahu rajulan, Abbas ibn Mirdas and al-Asha."}, {"id": "28:27/q39/p3", "position": "Bint al-Shati's preface records scholarly collaborators and gratitude.", "reasons": "It names al-Kannuni, al-Madghari, al-Rawandi and Suhayr's two theses and quotes 35:10."}, {"id": "28:27/q39/p4", "position": "Her iʿjāz study compares Itqan questions with earlier works and discusses poetry as Arabic evidence.", "reasons": "She finds parallels without proving dependence; Abd al-Baqi compiles Ibn Abbas answers and later writers follow Anbari."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q40", "question": "What grammatical role does 'an ashuq' have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q40/p1", "position": "The infinitive clause is the object governed by 'I intend'.", "reasons": "Samin al-Halabi states this iʿrāb."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q41", "question": "Why is the father's statement of his own righteousness acceptable?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q41/p1", "position": "Self-description for a practical or religious purpose is permissible; only boasting is blameworthy.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares Joseph's request at 12:55 and says Shuayb was showing Moses his character."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q42", "question": "What variant reading of the two terms is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q42/p1", "position": "Al-Hasan lightens the yāʾ of al-ajalayni and leaves it vowelless.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports this noncanonical reading of the following verse's reference to the two terms."}]}
{"id": "28:27/q43", "question": "What is reported of Moses's child from this marriage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:27/q43/p1", "position": "His wife bore a son named Jarthama.", "reasons": "Nawf al-Shami reports the name in al-Durr."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q01", "question": "How does the opening conjunction compare with the parallel wording in al-Shura?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q01/p1", "position": "Al-Qasas opens with waw, whereas the parallel in al-Shura opens with fa.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan cites this as an example of one particle being substituted for another."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q02", "question": "Who is addressed, and what are they given?", "turns_on": "Whether the general address is stated as applying to all recipients or specified by the surrounding address to Meccan opponents.", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q02/p1", "position": "The address concerns people generally and the beneficial worldly means, wealth, children, and pleasant goods they receive.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari names wealth and children; al-Baydawi says worldly means; Ibn Ashur says the context restricts the general wording to beneficial things because giving normally means granting a benefit. Al-Tabatabai glosses ita as giving, and Abu Hayyan specifies pleasant gifts in which people boast."}, {"id": "28:60/q02/p2", "position": "The direct addressees are Meccan unbelievers, especially Quraysh and its leaders, and the worldly goods in which they take pride.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Wahidi specify Meccan unbelievers and wealth or good that ends with their lives; Ibn Atiyya names wealth, sons, and strength; al-Qurtubi says either the goods or their owners depart; al-Wasit as reported by Bursevi calls the gifts worldly means. Islahi identifies the leaders, and Kuranyolu calls them Meccan polytheists."}]}

Al-Alusi says the noun signals brevity, reinforced by the contrast with abqa."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q07", "question": "How is mataʿ al-hayat al-dunya read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The nominative predicate versus the reported accusative verbal noun and temporal accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q07/p1", "position": "The nominative mataʿ is the predicate: it is an enjoyment of worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Samin supplies the implied pronoun huwa before mataʿ."}, {"id": "28:60/q07/p2", "position": "A variant accusative mataʿan treats it as a verbal noun and life as the time during which they enjoy it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the variant with al-hayata as a temporal accusative; al-Samin and al-Alusi likewise parse mataʿan as a verbal noun and life as a time expression."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q08", "question": "What is said about the name al-dunya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q08/p1", "position": "This life is near and low, short and finite beside the other life.", "reasons": "Sufyan says it is called dunya because it is near. Al-Biqai says the description as near and low implies the afterlife; al-Alusi says it suggests lowliness and short duration; al-Tabatabai contrasts its nearness and finite span with the eternal afterlife."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q09", "question": "What does zina mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q09/p1", "position": "It is an added beauty or ornament of bodies and other things.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it beautifies bodies or things; al-Tabatabai calls it an addition that makes something beautiful."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q10", "question": "Why does this verse mention adornment in the parallel expression absent from al-Shura?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q10/p1", "position": "Adornments fit al-Qasas because Qarun later appears before his people in his finery; al-Shura has no comparable scene.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai and the Maʿtarak al-aqran report both point to Qarun's appearance at 28:79."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q11", "question": "What does the verse say about worldly enjoyment and adornment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q11/p1", "position": "Worldly goods give temporary enjoyment and beauty during mortal life, then perish or cease to benefit their owners.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Wahidi say Meccan gifts end with their lives; al-Tabari says wealth and children cannot help at the return to God; al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Biqai, Bursevi, al-Alusi, and al-Tabatabai emphasize their finite duration. Al-Qurtubi notes that either the goods or the owner depart. Ibn Atiyya says the address belittles Quraysh's pride in wealth, sons, and strength. Ibn Kathir calls the adornment lowly and fleeting; Ibn Ashur says even the quality of the blessings is inferior. Al-Biqai adds that the world and its adornments were neither eternal in the past nor will last in the future. Study Quran connects worldly ornament to 33:28."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q12", "question": "How are people divided in their use of this world's enjoyment and adornment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q12/p1", "position": "Believers provision themselves for the next life, hypocrites adorn themselves, and disbelievers merely enjoy this life.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi both transmit this threefold division from Ibn Abbas."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q13", "question": "What is meant by what is with God?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase points to God's promised reward or, in the inward reading, to God Himself beyond the blessings.", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q13/p1", "position": "It is God's reward, Paradise, or the blessed afterlife prepared for believers and obedient people.", "reasons": "Yahya, al-Qurtubi, al-Alusi, and al-Tabatabai identify Paradise or the afterlife; al-Tabari specifies the reward God keeps for those who obey and are loyal; al-Wahidi says it is bliss for believers. Al-Biqai calls it the reward promised for obedience, and Ibn Kathir says it is prepared for the righteous."}, {"id": "28:60/q13/p2", "position": "For the elect, God Himself is better and more enduring than created blessings, even Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami distinguishes the ordinary hearers of the first statement from the elect who hear that God is better; al-Nasrabadhi says most worship blessings, while the rare worship the Benefactor, and separation by anything, even obedience or Paradise, cheats a person."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q14", "question": "In what sense is what is with God better?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q14/p1", "position": "Its reward and delight surpass worldly benefits in degree and quality, and sound judgment should prefer it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq calls it better recompense; al-Razi says its benefits are greater and unmixed with worldly harms, which predominate; al-Baydawi calls it complete delight and pleasure; al-Biqai says it is more pleasant, beautiful, and satisfying even if worldly pleasure has some good; Bursevi and al-Alusi say its pure pleasure lacks pain or worry; Ibn Ashur stresses the quality and completeness of its kinds of blessing. The Prophet's reported image in Ibn Kathir compares this world with a finger dipped into the sea and what it brings back; Study Quran reports R's speck-of-dust beside the sea comparison."}]}
{"id": "28:60/q15", "question": "In what sense is what is with God more lasting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q15/p1", "position": "The divine reward and afterlife endure forever without depletion, while every worldly benefit ends.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari explicitly says the reward does not run out; Ibn Ishaq calls it more enduring; Ibn al-Jawzi's lexicon gives baqiyyah the sense of permanence; al-Razi compares infinite afterlife with each person's tiny finite share of the world; al-Biqai says the afterlife is everlasting although it was not eternal in the past. {"id": "28:60/q17", "question": "What does the closing appeal to reason demand?", "turns_on": "The general force of the rebuke and the identification of its immediate addressees; the notes do not present these as mutually exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q17/p1", "position": "It rebukes the hearers for failing to reflect, distinguish the lasting good from fleeting goods, and choose faith, obedience, and the better afterlife.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil as transmitted by al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, al-Nasafi, Ibn al-Jawzi, and al-Qurtubi state that what lasts is preferable. {"id": "28:60/q21", "question": "How does this verse answer the surrounding objection to guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:60/q21/p1", "position": "It answers Quraysh's fear of losing worldly security, wealth, and influence by setting that possible loss beside the lasting reward of guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Razi calls it the third answer to the objection that following religion would cost worldly life; al-Tabatabai calls it a third answer to fear of being seized from their land in 28:57, even conceding the risk.
